text: Every Terraform working directory starts in a workspace literally named default, so you've been using one since Chapter 1 without ever typing the word. A workspace is Terraform's built-in way of keeping multiple, independent state files for the same configuration — the HCL files don't change, only which state file terraform plan and apply read from and write to. Create a dev workspace and a prod workspace from the same main.tf, and Terraform tracks two completely separate sets of real infrastructure, without duplicating a single line of code.

terraform workspace new dev creates a workspace and switches to it immediately — do the same for staging and prod. terraform workspace list shows every workspace that exists, with an asterisk on the active one. terraform workspace select switches without creating anything, and it's the command you'll run constantly, right before every plan or apply, to confirm which environment you're actually pointed at.

Terraform exposes the active workspace's name as terraform.workspace, readable anywhere in your config. Here, a locals map keys VM sizes by environment name, and lookup reads that map using terraform.workspace as the key. Select the prod workspace and this exact same main.tf names the resource group rg-myapp-prod and sizes the VM Standard_D2s_v3. Select dev and it produces rg-myapp-dev on a much smaller size — no duplicated files, no copy-pasted directories.

That's the whole workflow: create a workspace per environment, select the right one, let terraform.workspace drive naming and sizing inside HCL you only wrote once. It's genuinely convenient when environments are structurally identical and differ mainly in scale — same resources, different sizes, maybe a different instance count — and it means one terraform apply cycle per environment instead of several copy-pasted directories to keep in sync by hand.

But every workspace still shares the same backend, the same provider block, and usually the same credentials — nothing stops a terraform apply aimed at prod while you think you're in dev. Lesson 18 covers that risk directly: the real tradeoff between workspaces and fully separate state files, and when each one actually earns its keep.
